conclusion.justification: The report explicitly states 'Conclusion: No.' and concludes that the best available clinical evidence does not show CoQ10 improves Parkinson's movement symptoms or slows clinical decline.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
**Conclusion: No.** The best available clinical evidence does **not** show that coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) improves Parkinson’s movement symptoms or slows clinical decline.

Why the idea arose: an early, relatively small randomized dose-ranging trial in early Parkinson’s reported a *possible* slowing of functional decline, so it justified larger testing. Its design was randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, but it was not definitive.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12374491/

What resolved the question: the subsequent large, multicenter Phase III randomized trial of high-dose CoQ10 found it was safe and well tolerated but showed **“no evidence of clinical benefit.”** This is stronger evidence than the earlier signal because it was designed to confirm efficacy in a larger population.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24664227/?dopt=Abstract

Evidence syntheses likewise evaluate therapeutic trials rather than relying on biological rationale (CoQ10’s antioxidant/mitochondrial roles) or findings of lower CoQ10 levels in some people with Parkinsonism. A 2022 systematic review/meta-analysis specifically assessed CoQ10 treatment trials in Parkinson’s disease and parkinsonian syndromes.  
https://www.mdpi.com/2075-4426/12/6/975  
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10072-016-2757-9

So, CoQ10 should not be considered an evidence-based treatment for tremor, slowness, rigidity, or disease progression in Parkinson’s disease. Discuss any supplement use with the treating clinician, particularly alongside prescribed Parkinson’s medications.
